turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit. You look tired. What brings you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Check-up only. I didn't even want to come, she has dragged me. I'm tired, can we not stretch this.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I am staying with him, doctor, live-in carer only. He is slowing down at home, so I fixed the appointment.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): And the traffic was too much. Whole morning wasted. Please be quick.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will try to be quick. Any chest pain?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I came for a check-up, that is all.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Even when you climb the stairs, or walk fast?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): If I hurry I get a bit puffed, that is all. It is age, no?
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He stops on the staircase and holds the railing. I see it almost every day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): What fuss. One staircase. I am sixty-four, not a young fellow.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you stop like that, is there any feeling in the chest itself?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not pain. Well... actually a tight feeling, middle of the chest, like a squeeze. Been there two months — no, four months.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only with climbing or walking fast?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Most days if I climb or I walk fast. I slow down and it eases in a minute or two. A little breathlessness comes with it also.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does that tightness go to the arm or the jaw?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not the arm, not the jaw. It stays in the chest.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any sweating or nausea along with it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating. No nausea.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And palpitations, heart racing or skipping?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Heart doesn't do that.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Giddiness, or swelling of the feet?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No giddiness. Feet are fine. I just want to finish and go.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He gets irritable when he is tired, doctor. He was up very early.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): I follow. Which tablets are you actually taking?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the BP. Five milligrams — no, sorry, ten milligrams. One in the morning.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): And aspirin, seventy-five milligrams. On and off, not every single day.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): On and off is putting it kindly. He skips many days, some weeks only three or four tablets. I keep telling him.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it when I remember. Don't scold me here.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablet, cholesterol or sugar?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin they gave for cholesterol. Twenty milligrams — no, it was ten. I stopped it, it didn't suit me.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped fully, or you still take it sometimes?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Fully stopped, around a year back. Isosorbide was also written on an old slip — that I never took, not even once.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): True, doctor. That isosorbide bottle is still sealed in the cupboard.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you had the high BP?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve years... no, fifteen years. Since a long time.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any diabetes?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Last year the sugar test was normal.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me check the pressure. Hmm, one sixty-six over one hundred — the cuff was crooked, ignore that. Repeat is one fifty-eight over ninety-four. Pulse is eighty-four, regular.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Ankles are not swollen.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think aloud. Sixty-four, BP for many years, this tightness on stairs and fast walking — my working impression is angina. Provisional only, not confirmed.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to book an echocardiogram this week, together with the ECG.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not sitting for some long test. I am exhausted, I want to go home.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He will simply refuse and walk out, doctor. Kindly keep it smaller today.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I am changing that. No echocardiogram. We will do a resting ECG, and blood tests — fasting sugar, a lipid profile, and kidney function.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): ECG and blood, fine. Do it and finish.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Continue amlodipine ten milligrams every morning, don't skip that one. Aspirin seventy-five, please take it daily, not on and off.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the tightness comes at rest, or you start sweating with it, go to emergency straight away. Don't wait at home.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Emergency, yes, I heard. Anything else?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week with the reports. We will talk once we see them.
[SEG0050] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will bring him only. He forgets dates otherwise.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Kindly see reception on the way out — they will arrange the ECG and the blood tests before you leave.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

omissions.text: Exertional chest tightness eases within 1 to 2 minutes after slowing down/stopping.
No other heart racing or skipping sensations were reported in addition to no palpitations.
Past medication history missing: isosorbide had previously been prescribed on an old slip but the patient says he never took it at all, and the caregiver confirms the bottle is still sealed.
A prior blood pressure reading of 166/100 mmHg was obtained but discarded because the cuff was crooked; only the repeat reading was accepted.

An echocardiogram was initially planned for this week together with the ECG, but this was changed because the patient resisted longer testing and the caregiver requested a smaller plan; final plan was no echocardiogram.
There was explicit patient reluctance/refusal about undergoing a long test, influencing the investigation plan.
